n: Mark opens with no birth story — he jumps straight to the good news. “Gospel” means “good news,” and his first line announces who Jesus is: the Christ (the anointed one) and the Son of God.

f.g: Greek euangelion — good news, a joyful announcement.

n: Mark quotes Malachi’s promise of a messenger sent ahead to prepare the way. John the Baptist is that forerunner, clearing the road for the Lord’s arrival.

f.w: I send my messenger before thy face

n: This line comes from Isaiah: a voice in the desert calling people to get ready for the Lord. Like workers smoothing a road for a coming king, John prepares hearts.

f.w: The voice of one crying in the wilderness

n: John baptized out in the wilderness and called people to repent — to turn their lives toward God — so their sins could be forgiven. His baptism looked forward to Christ.

f.g: Remission = release, forgiveness, the cancelling of a debt.

n: Crowds streamed out from the countryside of Judea and from Jerusalem itself. They were baptized in the Jordan River and openly admitted their sins.

f.g: The main river of Israel, flowing from the Sea of Galilee south to the Dead Sea.

n: John’s rough clothing and simple desert food made him look like the prophet Elijah, who also wore hair clothing and a leather belt. His appearance itself was a message.

f.g: A leather belt.
Locusts (grasshoppers) were permitted food under the law of Moses.

n: John pointed away from himself. Untying sandals was a slave’s lowliest task, yet he said he wasn’t worthy even to do that for the One coming after him.

f.g: The strap or thong of a sandal.

f.w: There cometh one mightier than I

n: John’s baptism by water was real, but Jesus would bring something more: the gift of the Holy Ghost, which cleanses and transforms from within.

f.w: baptize you with the Holy Ghost

n: Jesus came south from his hometown of Nazareth and was baptized by John. Though sinless, he chose to be baptized to show obedience and set the pattern for all.
As Jesus came up out of the water, heaven opened and the Spirit came down on him in the sign of a dove. Here the Son, the Spirit, and (next verse) the Father all appear.
The Father’s voice declares his love and approval for his Son. Latter-day Saints see this scene as clear evidence that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are three distinct beings.
Right after his baptism, the Spirit led Jesus out into the desert. Mark uses vivid, urgent words — “immediately,” “straightway” — to keep his story moving fast.

f.g: Strongly sends out. In the parallel account the Joseph Smith Translation adds that Jesus went into the wilderness “to be with God.”

n: For forty days Jesus faced Satan’s temptations, alone among wild animals, yet cared for by angels. Mark gives only a short summary; Matthew and Luke give details.
After John was arrested, Jesus began his public ministry in Galilee, the northern region where he grew up, announcing God’s kingdom.
Jesus’ message in a nutshell: God’s promised time has arrived, his kingdom is close at hand, so turn to God and trust the good news.

f.w: repent ye, and believe the gospel

n: Walking along the Sea of Galilee, Jesus noticed two brothers at work fishing — Simon (later called Peter) and Andrew.

f.g: A freshwater lake about 13 miles long in northern Israel, home to a busy fishing trade.

n: Jesus used their own trade as a picture of their new calling: instead of gathering fish, they would gather people to God.
They didn’t hesitate. Leaving their nets meant leaving their livelihood, a striking act of trust.
A little farther on, Jesus saw another pair of brothers, James and John, sons of Zebedee, repairing their nets in their boat.

f.g: Not the same as James the Lord’s brother; this James was later martyred.

n: They too followed immediately. The mention of hired servants suggests Zebedee’s fishing business was fairly successful — they gave up something real.

f.g: Paid workers — a sign the family business was not poor.

n: Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the lake, became Jesus’ base. On the sabbath he taught in its synagogue, the local meeting house for scripture and prayer.

f.g: A town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee; Peter’s home was there.
A Jewish gathering place for reading scripture, prayer, and teaching.

n: People were amazed. The scribes usually taught by quoting earlier teachers, but Jesus spoke with his own authority, as one who truly knew.

f.g: Teaching.
Experts in the law of Moses who copied and interpreted scripture.

n: In the middle of the meeting, a man controlled by an evil spirit cried out. Darkness reacts when light enters the room.

f.g: An evil spirit, a follower of Satan.

n: The evil spirit recognized exactly who Jesus was — the Holy One of God — and feared him. Knowing who Jesus is is not the same as following him.

f.w: what have we to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “leave us alone; we have nothing in common.”

f.w: I know thee who thou art

n: Jesus didn’t want testimony from demons. With a simple command he silenced the spirit and ordered it out.

f.g: Be quiet; literally “be muzzled.”

n: The spirit left violently, shaking the man and shrieking, but it had to obey.

f.g: Thrown into convulsions.

n: The crowd was stunned. Even evil spirits obeyed Jesus’ word. His power matched his teaching — both carried real authority.
News about Jesus spread quickly through all of Galilee.
Leaving the synagogue, Jesus and his four new disciples went to the home Simon and Andrew shared.
Simon Peter’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. This detail shows Peter was married. “Anon” means right away.

f.g: At once, immediately.

n: Jesus took her hand and raised her up, and she was healed so completely that she got up and served them. Healing led to service.

f.g: Served, waited on them.

n: The sabbath ended at sunset. Then people were free to carry their sick, so they brought everyone who was ill or troubled by evil spirits.

f.g: Jewish days begin at sunset; carrying burdens was avoided until the sabbath ended.

n: It seemed as if the whole town crowded around the doorway of the house.
Jesus healed people with all kinds of illnesses. He would not let the evil spirits announce who he was; he chose his own timing for revealing himself.

f.g: Various, many different kinds.

n: After a long night of healing, Jesus rose before dawn to pray alone. Even the Son of God made private prayer a priority.

f.g: A lonely, deserted spot.

n: Simon and the others went searching for him.
When they found him, they reported that everyone was looking for him — expecting him to come back and keep healing in Capernaum.
Jesus instead chose to move on. His main purpose was to preach the gospel to as many towns as possible, not just to stay where he was popular.
He traveled through Galilee teaching in synagogues and freeing people from evil spirits.
A man with leprosy knelt and pleaded. He didn’t doubt Jesus’ power — only whether Jesus would want to help someone like him.

f.g: Someone with a serious skin disease; under the law he was unclean and had to live apart from others.

n: Moved with compassion, Jesus touched him — something nobody else would do for a leper. His answer, “I will,” shows the Savior’s willingness to heal.

f.g: Touching a leper normally made a person ceremonially unclean; here Jesus’ touch made the leper clean.

n: The healing was instant and complete.
Jesus firmly instructed him and sent him off quickly.

f.g: Strictly, sternly ordered.

n: Jesus told him to keep quiet and to follow the law of Moses by showing himself to a priest, who would officially declare him clean and let him return to society.
The man couldn’t contain his joy and told everyone. As a result, crowds became so large that Jesus had to stay in open country — yet people still found him.

f.g: Spread widely, make public.
